title: Severe acute malnutrition (India)
clinicalScenario: Fictitious teaching case: a 14-month-old with bilateral pedal oedema, MUAC 10.9 cm, lethargy and a cold body arrives at a district hospital. Check glucose and temperature first, then plan stabilisation.

evidenceAudit.scope: Children (under 5 years, with infant criteria under 6 months) with severe acute malnutrition in India: triage, facility stabilisation, rehabilitation and community follow-up. Not for adults.
findings: Primary sources: ICMR Standard Treatment Workflow on SAM with complications (October 2019) and MoHFW Operational Guidelines on Facility Based Management of SAM (2011), both opened in this task.
Doses and thresholds that differ between the two sources are shown in the comparison table, not merged.

India regional topic for Marifa India only. No Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) registration claim is made. India National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM) listing was not re-checked in this task. Check hospital formulary and product strength.
unverifiedSections: MoHFW 2011 was read from a non-government library copy (IndiaSpend); its Section 6 discharge criteria and Annexures 13–19 (feed volume charts, target-weight definition) were not in the retrievable text.
MoHFW 2011 shock flowchart (Section 5.3b) was flattened in the retrieved text; the step after a repeat 15 ml/kg bolus (septic-shock pathway) should be confirmed against the printed flowchart.
Starter and catch-up feed volume charts were not opened; the 130 ml/kg/day figure is from the ICMR STW only.
The ICMR STW states two oral amoxicillin doses (50 mg/kg and 40–45 mg/kg per dose); the medicine plan keeps each in its stated context.
Penicillin-allergy alternatives and renal/hepatic dose adjustments are not given by either source.
Pathophysiology bullets are explanatory and tied to the management rules they justify; they add no new numbers.
Current WHO 2023 wasting guideline and any newer MoHFW SAM/MAM protocol were not opened; check for an update before clinical approval.
Normal values are typical adult ranges unless labelled otherwise; local laboratory ranges apply.

pathophysiology.summary: Severe acute malnutrition is severe wasting or nutritional oedema in a child. Children with a complication, poor appetite or failed home treatment need facility care in two phases: stabilisation, then rehabilitation with catch-up feeding.
keyMechanisms: Slowed metabolism and poor cardiac reserve: fast or sodium-rich fluids cause fluid overload, so rehydration is slow and monitored and starter feeds are low in sodium and protein.
Low glucose and fat reserves with poor thermoregulation make hypoglycaemia and hypothermia common and linked; both are prevented with frequent day-and-night feeds.
Weakened immunity: serious infection may show no fever, so every child admitted with complicated SAM receives empirical antibiotics.
Potassium, magnesium and micronutrient (zinc, copper, folate, vitamin A) depletion is expected and replaced routinely; iron is withheld until the rehabilitation phase.
Recovery needs catch-up growth: energy-dense catch-up feeds drive weight gain, which is tracked daily in g/kg/day.

physicalSigns: Signs of dehydration or skin infection
redFlags: Shock: cold hands, slow capillary refill, weak fast pulse
Severe pallor or Hb below 4 g/dL
Infant under 6 months too weak to suckle
precipitants: Pneumonia, diarrhoea, sepsis or skin infection
Poor feeding and failed home-based treatment

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Anthropometry below normal but above the SAM cut-offs, no oedema; managed in the community.
Shock without a clear fluid-loss history, or no improvement after the first IV bolus; managed with maintenance fluid, antibiotic review and an inotrope (MoHFW 2011, Section 5.3b).
Persistent poor weight gain despite adequate intake; gastric aspirate CBNAAT and HIV rapid test.

differentials.condition: Underlying disease causing primary treatment failure
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: No appetite or persistent oedema by day 4: consider congenital abnormality, inborn error of metabolism, immune deficiency, organ dysfunction or malignancy.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: MUAC below 11.5 cm, or WHZ below −3 SD, or bilateral pitting oedema
MUAC below 11.0 cm; MoHFW 2011 also uses weight-for-length below −3 SD (length over 45 cm), visible severe wasting (length under 45 cm) or oedema of both feet
Body mass index (BMI)-for-age at or below −3 SD
Any listed complication, failed appetite test, oedema +++, failed home treatment, or caregiver unable to cope
No appetite by day 4; no loss of oedema by day 4; oedema on day 10; weight gain below 5 g/kg/day for 3 days on catch-up diet

clinicalManagement.title: Classify and decide where to treat
actions: Measure MUAC, weight and length/height; check both feet for pitting oedema; do the appetite test if there is no complication.
Good appetite and no medical complication: home-based treatment with oral amoxicillin and follow-up (ICMR STW, section Triage).

Admit to the facility or Nutrition Rehabilitation Centre (NRC) if any complication, failed appetite test, oedema +++, failed home treatment or the caregiver cannot care for the child at home (MoHFW 2011, Section 2, p. 35).
Infants under 6 months: admit if too weak to suckle, weight-for-length below −3 SD (length over 45 cm), visible severe wasting (length under 45 cm) or oedema of both feet (MoHFW 2011, Section 2).

Anorexia; fever 39 °C or above or hypothermia below 35 °C; persistent vomiting; severe dehydration; altered consciousness or convulsions; hypoglycaemia; severe anaemia; severe pneumonia; extensive skin infection needing intramuscular medicines.

clinicalManagement.title: Treat the emergency complications
actions: Hypoglycaemia (glucose below 54 mg/dL): alert child 50 ml 10% glucose or sucrose orally or by nasogastric (NG) tube; lethargic, unconscious or convulsing child 5 ml/kg 10% glucose intravenously (IV), then 50 ml 10% glucose by NG tube. Start starter feed 30 minutes later (MoHFW 2011, Section 5.1, p. 41).

Hypothermia: skin-to-skin with the mother or radiant warmer; feed 2-hourly (12 feeds in 24 hours). Severe hypothermia (rectal below 32 °C): warm humidified oxygen and 5 ml/kg 10% dextrose IV (MoHFW 2011, Section 5.2, p. 42).
Severe anaemia (Hb below 4 g/dL, or 4–6.5 g/dL with respiratory distress): 10 ml/kg whole blood or packed red cells over 3 hours with furosemide 1 mg/kg at the start (ICMR STW, section Anemia).
No improvement in hypoglycaemia, hypothermia or shock: transfer to a paediatric intensive care unit (ICU) (ICMR STW, sections Hypoglycemia and Hypothermia).

branches.condition: Shock (lethargic or unconscious with cold hands, slow capillary refill, weak fast pulse) — MoHFW 2011, Section 5.3b, pp. 44–45
actions: Oxygen, keep warm, IV access; 5 ml/kg 10% glucose IV.
Then 15 ml/kg over 1 hour of Ringer's lactate with 5% dextrose, half-normal saline with 5% glucose, or Ringer's lactate.
Improving (pulse and respiratory rate fall): switch to oral or NG oral rehydration solution (ORS) 10 ml/kg/hour for up to 10 hours and start starter feeds.

Not improving after the first bolus: repeat 15 ml/kg IV over 1 hour. Still not improving: treat as septic shock — maintenance IV fluid 4 ml/kg/hour, review antibiotics, start dopamine and re-feed as soon as possible; involve paediatric intensive care.

clinicalManagement.title: Rehydrate slowly when dehydrated without shock
actions: Reduced-osmolarity ORS 5 ml/kg every 30 minutes for 2 hours, then 5–10 ml/kg in alternate hours for up to 10 hours; MoHFW adds 15 ml potassium chloride per litre of ORS (MoHFW 2011, Section 5.3a, p. 43).

Check pulse and respiratory rate every 30 minutes. Stop ORS if both rise (pulse by 15 or more and respiratory rate by 5 or more), jugular veins engorge or the eyelids become puffy (MoHFW 2011, Section 5.3a).

clinicalManagement.title: Stabilisation phase: starter feeds, antibiotics, micronutrients
actions: Starter diet (F-75: 75 kcal and 0.9 g protein per 100 ml) in frequent small feeds; reduce to 100 ml/kg/day in gross oedema; use an NG tube if the child takes 80% or less of the amount offered (MoHFW 2011, Section 5.7). The ICMR STW gives at least 5 feeds a day and 130 ml/kg/day in stabilisation (see the comparison table).
Give empirical antibiotics to every admitted child with complicated SAM (Medicines: inpatient branch).
Start zinc, copper, folic acid, potassium, magnesium and vitamin A (Medicines: micronutrient branch). Do not give iron in this phase (MoHFW 2011, Section 5.6).
Monitor temperature, pulse, respiratory rate, feed intake, stools and daily weight; record a fluid-balance chart (ICMR STW, section Stabilisation phase).

clinicalManagement.title: Transition and rehabilitation: catch-up feeding
clinicalManagement.timeframe: From return of appetite until discharge
actions: Move to transition when oedema has begun to fall, appetite has returned, no NG tube or infusion is needed and the child is alert (MoHFW 2011, Section 4).

Catch-up diet (F-100: 100 kcal and 2.9 g protein per 100 ml): give the same volume as the starter diet for 2 days, then increase each feed by 10 ml a day until some is left; 8 feeds a day, which can be 5 catch-up feeds and 3 modified family meals (MoHFW 2011, Section 5.8).
Start iron 3 mg/kg/day after 2 days on the catch-up diet (MoHFW 2011, Section 5.6).
Target weight gain is 8 g/kg/day or more (MoHFW 2011, Annexure 4 and key terms E3).

clinicalManagement.title: Review for primary treatment failure
actions: Primary failure: no return of appetite by day 4, no loss of oedema by day 4, oedema still present on day 10, or weight gain below 5 g/kg/day for 3 consecutive days on the catch-up diet (ICMR STW, section Primary failure of treatment).

Look for an unrecognised congenital abnormality, inborn error of metabolism, immune deficiency including HIV, tuberculosis, major organ dysfunction or malignancy; refer to a higher-level facility if no cause is found (ICMR STW; MoHFW 2011 key terms E2).

clinicalManagement.title: Discharge to community follow-up
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At discharge and for the following weeks
actions: Discharge when clinically well and alert, medical complications and oedema resolved or resolving, appetite good and intake at least 75% of the 150–200 kcal/kg/day target (ICMR STW, section Criteria for discharge).

Anganwadi worker (AWW) home visits weekly for 4 weeks, then every 2 weeks; weekly weighing at the Anganwadi centre; Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) ensures return for scheduled NRC follow-up visits (MoHFW 2011, Section 1, pp. 19–20).

regimens.indication: Uncomplicated SAM with good appetite treated at home
regimens.patientGroup: Children 6–59 months with SAM, passed appetite test, no complication
adjustments: Paediatric: Paediatric weight-based dose as listed; for children only.
Penicillin allergy: Cited sources give no penicillin-allergy alternative for this age group; discuss with a paediatric infectious-diseases specialist before substituting.
CKD: Cited source gives no renal dose adjustment; check creatinine and urine output and follow the unit pharmacist's advice.
CLD: Cited source gives no hepatic dose adjustment.

monitoring: Appetite, weight and oedema at each follow-up visit; return at once if a complication develops.
contraindications: Any complication or failed appetite test needs facility care instead.

medicationPlan.note: India regional topic for Marifa India only. No Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) registration claim is made. India National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM) listing was not re-checked in this task. Check hospital formulary and product strength. Ampicillin and gentamicin are given together; ceftriaxone replaces them only after 48 hours without response or for a critically ill child; oral amoxicillin follows once oral intake is accepted. Fluids, glucose and feeds are in Clinical management.

guidelineComparison.title: SAM: ICMR Standard Treatment Workflow 2019 versus MoHFW facility operational guidelines 2011

values: Home-based: 50 mg/kg per dose twice daily for 7–10 days; inpatient oral step-down: 40–45 mg/kg per dose twice daily for 7 days (sections Triage and Infections).
Uncomplicated: 15 mg/kg 8-hourly for 5 days (Section 5.5, p. 47).
Ampicillin 50 mg/kg 6-hourly plus gentamicin 7.5 mg/kg once daily for 7–10 days.
Same drugs and doses for 7 days; add cloxacillin 100 mg/kg/day 6-hourly if staphylococcal infection is suspected.
Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg once daily for 7–10 days if no response in 48 hours or critically ill.
Septic shock or no improvement: cefotaxime 150 mg/kg/day in 3 doses or ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day in 2 doses, plus gentamicin.
IV dextrose normal saline 4 ml/kg/hour for 2–3 days with early oral feeds (section Stabilisation phase).
Oral rehydration without shock; IV only for shock (15 ml/kg over 1 hour) and 4 ml/kg/hour maintenance for suspected septic shock (Sections 5.3a–b).
Axillary below 35 °C or rectal below 35.5 °C.
At least 5 feeds a day; 130 ml/kg/day in stabilisation; increase to 150–200 kcal/kg/day over 2–3 days.
8–12 feeds over 24 hours; 100 ml/kg/day in gross oedema; volumes from reference charts (Section 5.7).
Primary failure if below 5 g/kg/day for 3 consecutive days on catch-up diet.
Acceptable weight gain 8 g/kg/day or more (Annexure 4, key terms E3).

guidelineComparison.note: Both are Indian national sources and are shown side by side, not merged. The medicine plan uses the ICMR STW (more recent) doses; the facility team must choose and document one regimen.

teaching.scope: Children (under 5 years, with infant criteria under 6 months) with severe acute malnutrition in India: triage, facility stabilisation, rehabilitation and community follow-up. Not for adults.
learningObjectives: Classify SAM with MUAC, WHZ and oedema, and decide between home and facility care.
Treat hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration and shock with SAM-specific rules.
Plan feeds, antibiotics and micronutrients through stabilisation and rehabilitation.
keyPoints: Bilateral pitting oedema alone means SAM.
Every admitted child with complicated SAM gets empirical antibiotics.
Rehydrate slowly and stop if pulse and breathing rise together.
No iron until the catch-up phase.
pitfalls: Giving standard fast IV rehydration to a child with SAM.
Starting iron in the first days.
Missing hypoglycaemia and hypothermia at night when feeds are spaced out.
Discharging without an Anganwadi and ASHA follow-up plan.

patientEducation: Explain the feeding plan: small frequent feeds day and night, and why the formula changes.

Explain that antibiotics and supplements are given even without fever.

Introduce home foods during rehabilitation and continue energy-dense family meals after discharge.

Paediatric intensive care for shock or unresolved hypoglycaemia or hypothermia.
National tuberculosis programme and ART centre when tests are positive.

Good appetite with intake at least 75% of the 150–200 kcal/kg/day target.
Caregiver trained and community follow-up arranged.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Anganwadi worker home visits weekly for 4 weeks, then every 2 weeks, with weekly weighing at the Anganwadi centre; ASHA ensures return for scheduled NRC follow-up visits (MoHFW 2011, Section 1, pp. 19–20).

title: Neonatal sepsis / possible serious bacterial infection (India)
clinicalScenario: Fictitious teaching case: a 9-day-old born at term at home stops feeding, has a temperature of 35.2 °C and grunting. Warm, check glucose, take a blood culture and start antibiotics.

evidenceAudit.scope: Newborns and young infants under 2 months (0–59 days) in India with suspected sepsis or possible serious bacterial infection (PSBI): facility care and the outpatient pathway when referral is not feasible. Not for older children or adults.
findings: Primary Indian sources opened in this task: ICMR Standard Treatment Workflows 'Sepsis in Neonates' and 'Neonatal Emergency Triage' (July 2020) and MoHFW Standard Treatment Guidelines for Common Respiratory Infections in Children (July 2016), which hold the young-infant PSBI doses.
WHO 2015 PSBI guideline (referral not feasible) is a labelled international supplement for outpatient eligibility, follow-up and fast breathing alone.

India regional topic for Marifa India only. No Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) registration claim is made. India National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM) listing was not re-checked in this task. Check hospital formulary and product strength.
unverifiedSections: The ICMR STW defers empirical drug choice to unit policy; the facility drugs and doses are from MoHFW 2016 Table 7.
ICMR STW duration mapping was read from a flowchart whose layout was scrambled in the retrieved text; confirm against the printed STW.
MoHFW 2016 gives cefotaxime 50 mg/kg every 6 hours in Annexure 4 and every 8 hours in the meningitis footnote; the plan keeps each in its stated context and flags it for pharmacist confirmation.
No ceftriaxone neonatal dose was found in the opened Indian sources, so ceftriaxone is not in the plan.
Normal CSF cell counts, platelet and electrolyte reference intervals were not given by the sources; laboratory neonatal intervals apply.
A newer MoHFW PSBI operational guideline or the 2025 NCDC–ICMR antimicrobial guideline neonatal content was not opened in this task (the NCDC PDF was unreadable to the retrieval tool).
Penicillin-allergy alternatives and renal/hepatic dose adjustments are not given by any source opened.
Normal values are typical adult ranges unless labelled otherwise; local laboratory ranges apply.

pathophysiology.summary: Possible serious bacterial infection is the bedside syndrome in an infant under 2 months that may be sepsis, meningitis or pneumonia. Signs are non-specific, so recognition, a blood culture and prompt antibiotics with planned stop points are the core of care.
keyMechanisms: Immature immunity makes signs non-specific: poor feeding, lethargy, temperature instability and apnoea may be the only clues.

Infection in the first days often follows maternal and birth exposure (prolonged rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis, unclean vaginal examination); later infection is linked to the home or nursery environment.
Sepsis can progress to shock and disseminated bleeding, and can seed the meninges, which changes the drug and the duration.
Hypoglycaemia and hypothermia accompany sepsis and must be corrected alongside antibiotics.
CRP and procalcitonin rise with infection but also with non-infective stress, so they are most useful to support stopping antibiotics.

symptoms: Refusal to feed or feed intolerance
physicalSigns: Severe chest indrawing, grunting or nasal flaring
Heart rate above 160/min for 1 hour at normal temperature
Capillary refill over 3 seconds, mottled skin
redFlags: Respiratory distress needing intubation or Silverman score above 6
Respiratory distress starting more than 6 hours after birth
Unable to feed at all or persistent vomiting
precipitants: Rupture of membranes for 18 hours or more, or preterm prelabour rupture
Maternal fever, urinary infection, diarrhoea, chorioamnionitis or foul-smelling discharge
Unclean vaginal examination or unskilled birth attendant handling
Lapses in hand hygiene and asepsis in the nursery

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Temperature corrects with environment change and no other sign; temperature change not explained by the environment is a sepsis sign.
Low glucose or calcium; seizures stop with correction (ICMR Neonatal Emergency Triage).
Abdominal distension, bilious vomiting or a visible malformation; needs referral, not outpatient antibiotics (WHO 2015 critical illness).
Raised CRP with sterile blood culture, normal CSF and a well baby; supports stopping antibiotics.

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise PSBI and classify risk
actions: Young infant (under 2 months) with any of: convulsions, fast breathing (60/min or more), severe chest indrawing, nasal flaring, grunting, not feeding, bulging fontanelle, lethargy or unconsciousness, reduced movement, temperature 37.5 °C or above or below 35.5 °C = possible serious bacterial infection (PSBI) (MoHFW 2016, Table 6, p. 8).

Facility newborns: high probability of sepsis with any red flag, two yellow signs or maternal risk factors, or one with gestation 32 weeks or less; one yellow sign or risk factor above 32 weeks = at risk: observe for 48–72 hours without antibiotics (ICMR STW Sepsis in Neonates).
Shock; bleeding from several sites; respiratory distress needing intubation or Silverman score above 6; respiratory distress starting more than 6 hours after birth.

Heart rate above 160/min for 1 hour despite normal temperature; respiratory distress; lethargy; refusal to feed or feed intolerance; new apnoea; seizures; floppiness; fever or hypothermia not explained by the environment.

clinicalManagement.title: Stabilise: temperature, airway, breathing, circulation, glucose
actions: Keep warm: skin-to-skin or a servo-controlled warmer; severe hypothermia (below 32 °C) also needs IV fluids and vitamin K injection (ICMR Neonatal Emergency Triage).
Oxygen if SpO2 below 91%; CPAP for respiratory distress; follow neonatal resuscitation for apnoea or gasping (ICMR Neonatal Emergency Triage).
Shock: normal saline 10 ml/kg IV over 30–60 minutes, repeat if volume deficit persists, consider inotropes (ICMR Neonatal Emergency Triage).
Glucose below 45 mg/dL: feed if asymptomatic; if symptomatic or below 20 mg/dL give 10% dextrose (Medicines: supportive branch).

clinicalManagement.title: Culture, then start antibiotics
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Within the first hour of recognition
actions: Take a blood culture before the first dose; admit to the special newborn care unit (SNCU) or neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) (ICMR STW).

No meningitis suspected: ampicillin plus gentamicin. Meningitis suspected (bulging fontanelle, seizures, staring spells, altered sensorium): cefotaxime plus gentamicin and an LP when stable (MoHFW 2016, pp. 9–10).
Do not start antibiotics without an indication in an at-risk baby; observe 48–72 hours and start if a further yellow or red sign appears (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Review at 48 hours
actions: Stop if sepsis signs have gone and CRP is 12 mg/L or below, or the blood culture is sterile at 48 hours and the baby has recovered (ICMR STW).
No improvement: change to cefotaxime with or without gentamicin for 10–14 days (MoHFW 2016, p. 9).

clinicalManagement.title: Day-5 review and total duration
actions: Stop at day 5 if well for the last 48 hours with sterile blood culture and normal CSF (ICMR STW).

Planned durations: pneumonia 5–7 days; CRP above 12 mg/L with sterile culture and normal CSF 5–7 days; culture-positive sepsis 10–14 days; meningitis about 21 days (ICMR STW; mapping from the flowchart).

clinicalManagement.title: When referral is refused or not possible
actions: Exclusions: birth weight below 1.5 kg (1500 g), hospital stay for illness in the previous 2 weeks, or any critical-illness sign — these infants must be treated in hospital (WHO 2015, p. 16).

Clinical severe infection: gentamicin IM once daily plus oral amoxicillin for 7 days; give the first doses as pre-referral treatment and keep the infant warm and fed (MoHFW 2016, p. 7; WHO 2015 Recommendation 4).
Fast breathing alone: 7–59 days, oral amoxicillin for 7 days without referral; 0–6 days, refer, and use the same amoxicillin only if referral is refused (WHO 2015 Recommendations 2–3).
Follow up on day 4. Refer at once for any critical-illness sign, a new sign after 48 hours, or any sign still present on day 8 (WHO 2015, pp. 16 and 22).

Unconscious, convulsions, unable to feed at all, apnoea, unable to cry, cyanosis, bulging fontanelle, active bleeding, surgical condition, persistent vomiting: give pre-referral ampicillin and gentamicin and hospitalise.

clinicalManagement.title: Discharge and prevention
actions: Discharge when feeding well, temperature stable and antibiotics complete or stopped by the rules above.
Unit prevention: hand hygiene, asepsis and housekeeping (ICMR STW, section Prevention).

medicationPlan.note: India regional topic for Marifa India only. No Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) registration claim is made. India National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM) listing was not re-checked in this task. Check hospital formulary and product strength. Ampicillin and the aminoglycoside are given together; cloxacillin is added only for suspected staphylococcal infection; cefotaxime replaces ampicillin for meningitis or after 48 hours without improvement. Every course has a 48-hour review and a stop date.

guidelineComparison.note: Sources are shown side by side, not merged. The medicine plan follows MoHFW 2016 for Indian facility and outpatient doses and WHO 2015 only for fast breathing alone, which MoHFW 2016 does not separately cover. The unit must choose and document one regimen.

teaching.scope: Newborns and young infants under 2 months (0–59 days) in India with suspected sepsis or possible serious bacterial infection (PSBI): facility care and the outpatient pathway when referral is not feasible. Not for older children or adults.
learningObjectives: Recognise PSBI signs and classify sepsis risk in a young infant.
Start the right antibiotics after a blood culture and stop them by the 48-hour and day-5 rules.
Know who can be treated as an outpatient when referral is not feasible, and when to refer.
keyPoints: Signs are subtle: feeding, movement and temperature matter.
Blood culture before the first dose.
Infants under 1.5 kg or critically ill always need hospital care.
pitfalls: Continuing antibiotics for 7 days in a well baby with a sterile culture and low CRP.
Missing meningitis by not doing an LP once the baby is stable.
Treating fast breathing in a 3-day-old as an outpatient without first offering referral.

patientEducation: Teach danger signs: not feeding, reduced movement, fast breathing, chest indrawing, feeling hot or cold, convulsions — return at once.
Explain the antibiotic plan, the 48-hour review and the stop date.
Outpatient pathway: explain the daily injection visits and the day-4 review.
lifestyleAndDiet: Continue exclusive breastfeeding; give expressed breast milk if the infant cannot suckle.
Keep the baby warm with skin-to-skin contact; wash hands before handling.
mdtReferrals: ANM and ASHA for outpatient injections and home follow-up when referral is not feasible.
dischargeCriteria: Feeding well by breast or cup.
Antibiotic course completed or stopped by the stop rules.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Outpatient pathway: review on day 4 and refer for any critical-illness sign, a new sign after 48 hours or any sign still present on day 8 (WHO 2015). After facility discharge: routine newborn follow-up with hearing screening where aminoglycosides were used, per unit policy.
